about: nxk dogfood run: a made-up budgeting app called Tally. Values are average model support (%) from Jev (jev-latest) over PersonaGen UK profiles. Option order was rotated between people.

rounds.context: Think about how you keep track of your money from day to day: what you spend, what's coming out and what's left until you're next paid.
rounds.question: Over the next three months, what are you most likely to do about keeping track of your spending?

rounds.context: You come across the website of a new budgeting app called Tally and read the whole page. The headline says: 'Take control of your finances with AI-powered insights.' Below it are three points: 'Smart categorisation', 'Personalised insights' and 'Bank-level security'. The button says 'Start your free trial'. The small print says: '30 days free, then £4.99 a month. Connect your bank with Open Banking.' The page says nothing else.
rounds.question: Having read the page, what would you do?

rounds.context: You come across the website of a new budgeting app called Tally and read the whole page. The headline says: 'Take control of your finances with AI-powered insights.' Below it are three points: 'Smart categorisation', 'Personalised insights' and 'Bank-level security'. The button says 'Start your free trial'. The small print says: '30 days free, then £4.99 a month. Connect your bank with Open Banking.' The page says nothing else.
rounds.question: What, if anything, would most put you off starting the free trial?

rounds.context: A budgeting app connects to your bank account through Open Banking so it can see your balance, incoming pay, bills and spending. It can only offer one of the features below to start with.
rounds.question: Which one feature would be most useful to you?

rounds.context: A new budgeting app connects to your bank account through Open Banking (read-only; it cannot move your money). Every morning it tells you how much you can safely spend that day until payday, after your bills are covered, and it warns you a few days before a payment would take you overdrawn or bounce. It comes in the versions below.
rounds.question: Which version, if any, would you start using?

rounds.context: You've been using the free version of a budgeting app for a month. Every morning it tells you how much you can safely spend that day until payday, after your bills are covered. It connects to your bank read-only and cannot move your money. The app offers an upgrade that warns you a few days before a payment would take you overdrawn or bounce, and flags forgotten subscriptions. The upgrade costs £2.99 a month, cancel any time.
rounds.question: What would you do about the upgrade?

rounds.context: You see the website for a new budgeting app. Under the headline, the page says: 'Every morning, Tally checks your balance, bills and payday, and tells you what's safe to spend. It warns you before a payment would take you overdrawn. Free to use. Read-only: it can't move your money.' The only difference between versions of the page is the headline.
rounds.question: Which headline would make you most likely to try the app?

rounds.context: You see the website for a new budgeting app called Tally. It connects to your bank read-only and cannot move your money. Free: every morning it tells you how much you can safely spend that day until payday, after your bills are covered. Upgrade, £2.99 a month: it warns you a few days before a payment would take you overdrawn or bounce, and finds subscriptions you've forgotten about. Any month the upgrade doesn't save you at least £2.99 in avoided overdraft, late-payment or forgotten subscription charges, you get that month's £2.99 back automatically. Cancel any time.
rounds.question: Imagine you have used the free version for a month. Would you pay for the upgrade?

rounds.context: You see the website for a new budgeting app called Tally. It connects to your bank read-only and cannot move your money. Free: every morning it tells you how much you can safely spend that day until payday, and it warns you a few days before a payment would take you overdrawn or bounce. Upgrade, £2.99 a month: it finds subscriptions and direct debits you've forgotten about, cancels them for you, and alerts you before any price rise or free trial turns into a charge. Any month the upgrade doesn't save you at least £2.99 in avoided overdraft, late-payment or forgotten subscription charges, you get that month's £2.99 back automatically. Cancel any time.
